source.title: Zero Variance Portfolio
source.authors: Jinyuan Chang; Yi-Peng Ding; Zhen-Tao Shi; Bo Zhang

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests double-descent-like portfolio-risk behavior by sweeping asset count and sample size, using minimum-variance portfolio estimators rather than deep-network test error.
record.gate_note: The paper's own risk curves and simulations bear on double descent in portfolio optimization. The prose cites double-descent results from other work, which are not recorded as findings here. The paper also reports results for other portfolio estimators, but the extracted size-sweep table rows below are limited to ZVP1; the optimally tuned ridge comparison is included because the text says it flattens the peak.
record.test_reason: The paper's own simulations, theory and S&P 500 data show that portfolio risk falls, peaks at N = T, and falls again for the minimum-norm interpolating minimum-variance portfolio (ZVP). It also sweeps sample size T at fixed N and compares an optimally tuned ridge. This is a new setting (portfolio optimization, not deep nets) with results on V3, V4, V5 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the minimum-norm zero variance portfolio generalizes out of sample and shows double descent in risk, with the peak at N = T. They find the pseudoinverse estimator fails to interpolate and diverges from optimality. ZVP1 asymptotically matches optimally tuned ridge when N ≫ T. The refined ZVP2 attains oracle risk when the idiosyncratic covariance can be estimated consistently, and it performs competitively on S&P 500 and Nikkei data.
record.recipe_differences: This is a minimum-variance portfolio estimator study, not a deep-network experiment. It varies asset count or sample size and measures portfolio risk; it does not measure neural-network test error.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported shape varies with the swept axis and finite-sample setting: the fixed-T asset sweep has a renewed rise at N = 1000, while the fixed-N sample-size sweep peaks at T = N. The paper says tuned ridge flattens the interpolation bump.
record.problems: The main Figure 4 curves average 10 replications for brevity; no uncertainty bars are stated for those curves. The tabulated simulation results report means and standard deviations over 1000 replications, but the study concerns a portfolio-risk measure rather than neural-network test error. The reported size sweep also has a high-N rebound in one simulation setting.
record.rows_left_out: Left out the corresponding ZVP1 values in Tables 1 and 3 (Setting 1, identity idiosyncratic covariance), other portfolio methods in the simulation tables, and additional empirical table metrics. The extracted table rows prioritize Setting 2 results because the paper specifically discusses its size-related RR deterioration; the figure rows capture the directly described double-descent sweeps.

untested.parts: No training-time or epoch axis is studied.
The epoch axis is not tested; the only complexity measure used is N/T.
The paper does not test whether label noise drives the peak, and no triple or multiple descent is examined.

missing.what: Asymptotic relative variance of ZVP: 1/(1−γ) for γ < 1, γ/(γ−1) for γ > 1 (isotropic Ω), and → 1 as N/T → ∞. This is an analytic double-descent curve with its peak at γ = 1.
Pseudoinverse weight: risk diverges after N > 50 in simulation and is worst in empirical risk (e.g. 0.226 vs 0.133 for ZVP1 at T = 22).
Proposition 2: when N ≫ T, the best-tuned ridge risk is asymptotically equal to ZVP risk. OptRidge equals ZVP1 for N ≥ 50, and its chosen penalties are virtually zero.
Multinational pool (about 725 stocks) lowers risk for all estimators except the pseudoinverse (ZVP2 0.097 → 0.084 at T = 22).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'challenges' label on the T2/T4 rows is removed. Those rows report RR, which is relative to an oracle risk that itself falls with N, and they cover only N > T, so they cannot show risk rising. The F5–F8 labels change from limits_scope to supports, because the missing first descent is untested, not a qualification. The tranche is T3 (new setting with a result on the claim) rather than T2.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks and their test error are not studied.
No training-epoch or training-time sweep is performed.
The sample-size sweep is for the portfolio problem and its risk measure, not neural-network test error.
The paper studies portfolio estimators, not a broad range of model classes; the reported behavior is not established as universal.
The paper examines asset-count and sample-size axes through N/T; it does not test epochs or establish a universal effective-complexity measure across settings.
It compares optimally tuned ridge near the interpolation region but does not test whether label noise drives the peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimal regularization generally removes them.
No comparison against an effective parameter count or demonstration of an ordinary U-shaped curve under such a count.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Pseudoinverse estimator instead of the minimum-norm ZVP
source_check.reason: Section 1.1 reports only a brief second descent before pseudoinverse risk diverges from the oracle beyond N = 50. This qualifies the estimator choice; the pseudoinverse portfolio also fails to interpolate.

relationships.condition: ZVP1, Setting 2, sweeps over N (T = 22) and over T (N = 500)
relationships.reason: On both axes the peak sits at N/T = 1, the interpolation threshold (F2, F3). Theorem 1 gives RV → 1/(1−γ) and γ/(γ−1) on either side of γ = 1.
relationships.display_finding: Both sweeps peaked at N/T=1; Theorem 1 gives RV→1/(1−γ) below γ=1 and RV→γ/(γ−1) above it, with the latter requiring isotropic idiosyncratic covariance.
